q: What is Salesforce Data 360?
alt: Can you explain Data 360 in simple words?
What is data 360 in salesforce and why do companies use it
Tell me about Salesforce's data platform, the one that used to be Data Cloud
what does data three sixty do
a: Data 360 is Salesforce's data platform. It brings customer data from lots of systems into one place, harmonizes it to a common model, and unifies it into a single profile per customer. It used to be called Data Cloud and was renamed Data 360 at Dreamforce 2025, and it now sits under Agentforce 360 as the data layer for agents. Say a retailer has the same shopper in its online store, its loyalty app and Service Cloud. Data comes in through data streams, lands in data lake objects, gets mapped to data model objects, and identity resolution builds one unified profile for that shopper. On top of that you build calculated insights, segments, activations and data actions. And you can ground Agentforce and Prompt Builder with that data, including unstructured content through search indexes. So the agent helping that shopper actually knows who they are.

Renamed at Dreamforce 2025, part of Agentforce 360

q: What is the difference between a Data Lake Object and a Data Model Object?
alt: DLO vs DMO in Data 360
Explain DLO and DMO
what is d l o and d m o
Why do we need both data lake objects and data model objects?
a: A Data Lake Object, or DLO, stores data as it arrives from a source, in that source's own shape and field names. A Data Model Object, or DMO, is the harmonized, standard view of the data, based on the Customer 360 Data Model, like Individual, Contact Point Email or Sales Order. You map DLO fields to DMO fields. So say the CRM calls it Email, the online store calls it customer_email and the loyalty system calls it mail_id. Each one lands in its own DLO as is, and all three map to the same field on the Contact Point Email DMO. Identity resolution, calculated insights, segments, activation and agent grounding all work on DMOs, not on raw DLOs. So the DLO is the storage layer and the DMO is the business-friendly, unified layer. Quick way to spot them: DMOs end with __dlm in their API names, and DLOs end with __dll.

q: How does data mapping work in Data 360 and what must you map for identity resolution?
alt: What is data mapping in data 360
What are the mandatory mappings in Data 360?

a: Data mapping is where I connect each DLO field to the matching field on a standard or custom DMO, so data from different sources speaks the same language. For identity resolution to work, I have to map person data to the Individual DMO, including the Individual Id. I also map at least one way to match people, like Contact Point Email, Contact Point Phone, Contact Point Address, or Party Identification for things like loyalty or customer numbers. Those contact point objects must carry the Party field that links back to the Individual. For example, when I map a loyalty member file, the member number goes into Party Identification and the email into Contact Point Email, and both point back to the same Individual Id. I also make sure the primary key is set and the relationships between DMOs are defined, because segments and insights rely on those relationships.

a: The Customer 360 Data Model is Salesforce's standard set of data model objects and relationships that Data 360 uses to harmonize data from any source. It's organized into subject areas. q: What are the data stream categories Profile, Engagement and Other?

a: When I create a data stream I choose a category, and that tells Data 360 how the data behaves. Profile is for data about who someone is, like contacts, leads or loyalty members, and it's usually mapped to Individual and contact points. Engagement is for time-stamped events like web visits, email opens or purchases. So it needs an event date field, and it's used for things like recency in segments and insights. Other covers everything else, like product catalogs or store lists. For a retailer it's easy to picture: loyalty members are Profile, online purchases are Engagement, and the store list is Other. The category matters because it affects how the data is stored and partitioned and which features can use it. And you can't change the category of a data lake object after it's created, so I decide it carefully up front.

q: What is identity resolution in Data 360?
alt: How does Data 360 create a single customer profile?
Explain identity resolution
what is a unified profile and how is it built
how does data 360 know two records are the same person
a: Identity resolution takes records about the same person from different sources and links them into one unified profile. I configure a ruleset with match rules, which decide when two records are the same person, for example exact email, or fuzzy first name plus exact last name plus normalized phone. Then reconciliation rules decide which value wins for each attribute when sources disagree, like most recent or a source priority order. Say Priya Sharma exists in CRM, and P. Sharma signed up on the website with the same email. The email rule links them, and if their addresses differ, reconciliation picks one, for example the most recent. The result is the Unified Individual DMO plus link objects that connect each unified profile back to its source records. Segments, insights and agents then work on that unified profile instead of on duplicates.
points: Ruleset = match rules + reconciliation rules
Creates Unified Individual and unified link objects
Source records are linked, not deleted
Foundation for segments and personalization

q: What is the difference between match rules and reconciliation rules?
alt: Match rules vs reconciliation rules in identity resolution
How do reconciliation rules decide which value wins?
what are the match methods in data 360
Explain exact, fuzzy and normalized matching
a: Match rules decide whether two source records belong to the same person. Reconciliation rules decide which attribute values the unified profile shows. A match rule is a set of criteria that must all be true, like exact normalized email, or fuzzy first name plus exact last name plus exact phone. You can have several match rules, and any one of them can link records. Reconciliation rules work at the field level: last updated, most frequent, or source priority, where I rank sources, say CRM above web forms. So if a web form has one phone number and CRM has another, source priority means the profile shows the CRM number. In practice I start strict, check the consolidation rate and sample unified profiles, and only loosen rules when I can prove they're not merging different people.

Criteria inside a rule are ANDed; rules are ORed

That matters for segments built on the unified profile, for data graphs, and for showing unified data on a CRM record. Source records are never deleted or overwritten. q: What is a calculated insight in Data 360?
alt: Explain calculated insights

calculated insight example
a: A calculated insight is a reusable metric defined on Data 360 data, usually at the unified profile level, like customer lifetime value, total orders in the last 90 days, or average case count. I build it with SQL or the visual builder. I define measures, which are the aggregated numbers, and dimensions, which are what I group by, like Unified Individual Id. It runs in batch on a schedule over the full history, and the results land in a calculated insight object. For example, a retailer might define total orders in the last 90 days once, then use it for a VIP segment, show it on the CRM contact, and let an agent refer to it. That's the point: you can use it in segments, activation, data actions, flows, CRM enrichment and agent grounding. Define the metric once and reuse it everywhere, instead of recalculating it in every report.

q: What is the difference between calculated insights and streaming insights?
alt: Calculated vs streaming insights in Data 360
When would you use a streaming insight?
real time insights in data 360
batch insight vs streaming insight
a: Calculated insights run in batch over the full historical data, so they are perfect for long-term metrics like lifetime value, loyalty tier or purchase frequency, and they can join across unified profiles. Streaming insights are computed on events as they arrive, inside a time window, like counting product views in the last fifteen minutes, so latency is seconds to minutes. Streaming insights cannot look at lifetime history the way a calculated insight can, but they pair well with data actions to react immediately, for example triggering a cart-abandonment follow-up. My rule is: use calculated insights to understand and segment customers, and streaming insights to trigger something right now. Streaming also tends to consume more credits, so I only use it when timing really matters.
points: Calculated: batch, historical, joins to profiles
Streaming: windowed, near real time

I create it in the segment builder. I choose what I'm segmenting on, usually Unified Individual, then drag in attributes from the profile, related DMOs like orders or engagement, and calculated insights. A segment refreshes on a publish schedule and then gets activated to targets like Marketing Cloud, advertising platforms or cloud storage. One thing I always point out: segments are only as good as the unified profiles behind them, so identity resolution quality matters.

q: What are data actions in Data 360?

a: A data action fires when a record in a DMO or an insight changes and meets conditions I define, and it sends an event to a target. For example, when a streaming insight shows a high-value customer has viewed the same product several times, a data action can publish a platform event, and a platform-event-triggered flow or Apex subscriber creates a task for the account owner. The difference from activation is that activation sends audiences in batches, while a data action is event-driven and near real time for one record. I keep the payload small and make the subscriber idempotent, because events can arrive more than once.

q: What is zero copy and data federation in Data 360?
alt: Explain zero copy integration with Snowflake
How does Data 360 work with Databricks without copying data?
what is data federation in data 360
zero copy partner network
query federation vs file federation
a: Zero copy lets Data 360 use data that lives in an external platform like Snowflake, Databricks, Google BigQuery or Amazon Redshift, without copying it into Data 360. Inbound is called federation. Data 360 queries the external tables live, either through query federation, where the warehouse runs the query, or file federation, where Data 360 reads the open-format files directly. The external data shows up as a data lake object that I can map, unify and segment like any other, and there's optional caching for performance. Outbound, Data 360 can share its data, like unified profiles and insights, back to those platforms without exports. For example, if a bank keeps years of transaction history in Snowflake, I can segment on it in Data 360 without building a copy pipeline, and share the unified profiles back to the data team. The benefit is no duplicate pipelines and one source of truth.

q: When would you federate data with zero copy versus ingest it into Data 360?
alt: Zero copy or ingestion, how do you decide?
Should we copy our Snowflake data into Data 360 or federate it?
pros and cons of data federation
how to decide between federation and data streams
a: I decide based on freshness, query frequency, volume, cost and ownership. I federate when the data already lives and is governed in a warehouse like Snowflake or Databricks, it is large, and Data 360 only needs part of it or needs it occasionally, because that avoids duplicate pipelines and storage. I ingest when the data is used constantly in identity resolution, frequent segments or real-time use cases, because querying the same external tables over and over can cost more credits and warehouse compute than ingesting once. I also look at latency, whether the external platform can handle the query load, and network setup like private connectivity. Often it is hybrid: CRM and engagement data ingested, big history and finance data federated, with caching where needed.
points: Federate: big, warehouse-governed, occasional use
Ingest: heavy, repeated, real-time use

q: How does Data 360 handle unstructured data, and what is the difference between vector and hybrid search indexes?
alt: What is a search index in Data 360?
vector search vs hybrid search in data 360
How does Data 360 store PDFs and documents for AI?
what is chunking and embedding in data 360
a: Data 360 can ingest unstructured content like PDFs, knowledge articles, transcripts and web pages. It maps that to unstructured data model objects, splits it into chunks and creates vector embeddings, all stored in a search index. A vector index does semantic search. It finds chunks that mean the same thing as the question even if the words differ, so it works well for longer natural questions. A hybrid index combines vector search with keyword search and merges the results, which helps when questions include exact terms like product codes or error numbers. So 'my printer keeps jamming' suits vector search, but 'what does error E-204 mean' needs the keyword side of hybrid. There's also an enriched option that adds summaries, keywords and likely questions to chunks for better retrieval, at extra credit cost. Retrievers then query these indexes to ground prompts and agents.
points: Ingest, chunk, embed, index
Vector: meaning-based
Hybrid: meaning plus exact keywords
Retrievers sit on top of the index

q: How does Data 360 ground Agentforce agents and prompts?

a: Data 360 grounds agents in two main ways. For unstructured knowledge, content is chunked and indexed in a search index, and a retriever queries that index. A prompt template or the agent's knowledge action uses the retriever to fetch the most relevant chunks and adds them to the prompt. That's retrieval augmented generation. For structured data, agents and prompts can use unified profile attributes, calculated insights or data graphs, like a customer's loyalty tier or recent orders, through actions, flows, Apex or prompt template resources. So when a customer asks a service agent whether they can return a jacket, it pulls the return policy chunk from the index, and the customer's recent order and loyalty tier from the profile. The Agentforce Data Library sets up the stream, index and retriever for you when you point it at knowledge articles or files. And all of this goes through the Einstein Trust Layer.

q: How would you reduce Data 360 credit consumption on an implementation?
alt: Our Data 360 credits are burning too fast, what would you do?
Data 360 cost optimization tips
how to optimize data 360 consumption

a: First I open Digital Wallet to see which usage types and features are consuming the most, because it is usually a few things like identity resolution, frequent segment refreshes or streaming. q: What is the difference between Data 360, normal CRM data and a CDP?

a: CRM data is the transactional system of record: accounts, contacts, cases and opportunities that users create and edit every day, with sharing, validation and automation. It's built into the Salesforce metadata layer, so its data can be used in flows, Apex, record pages, Prompt Builder and Agentforce, plus zero copy with warehouses and unstructured data for AI. Think of a retailer: the service case lives in CRM, the millions of website clicks live in Data 360, and Data 360 data can show up on that case's record page. q: What is the Atlas Reasoning Engine?

a: The Atlas Reasoning Engine is the brain behind Agentforce. When a user sends a message, it understands the intent, picks the right subagent, plans which actions to run, runs them, looks at the results, and decides whether it has enough to answer or needs another step. Then it writes the response. For example, a customer asks to change the delivery address on their last order. Atlas routes to the order subagent, runs a lookup action, looks at what comes back, decides it needs one more step, runs the update action, and then confirms. It uses large language models along with the agent's descriptions, instructions, variables and grounding data. In the new Agentforce Builder, Atlas runs on an enhanced graph-based engine that supports hybrid reasoning. So some steps follow a fixed path every time, and others are left to the model's judgment. q: What is the Einstein Trust Layer?

a: The Einstein Trust Layer is the set of security and governance controls that every Agentforce and Prompt Builder request passes through. On the way in, it grounds prompts with data the user is allowed to see, masks sensitive data like personal information before it reaches the model (for prompt templates and features like Service Replies; Salesforce turned masking off for Agentforce agents because it slowed them down and hurt accuracy, and relies on zero data retention and access controls there), and adds prompt defense to reduce injection and misuse. Salesforce has zero data retention agreements with its model providers, so prompts and responses aren't stored or used to train their models. On the way back, it scans responses for toxicity, unmasks the data, and records an audit trail, including prompts, responses and feedback, in Data 360. So say a rep asks for a summary of a customer's case. The model doesn't see the customer's personal details in clear text, the reply is checked before the rep sees it, and there's a record of what was asked. That's the reason companies can use generative AI with their CRM data safely.

q: How do data masking and zero data retention work in the Einstein Trust Layer?

a: Data masking detects sensitive values in the prompt, like names, emails, phone numbers or card numbers, plus fields classified as sensitive, and replaces them with placeholder tokens before the prompt leaves Salesforce. The model works with the placeholders. When the response comes back, the Trust Layer puts the real values back in before showing it to the user. So if a case mentions a customer's name and email, the model only sees placeholders, and the user still sees the real name and email in the reply. Admins can configure which entity types are masked. Big gotcha in interviews: this masking applies to prompt templates and features like Service Replies, but Salesforce turned it off for Agentforce agents, because it added latency and hurt the planner's accuracy. For agents, protection comes from zero data retention, guardrails and what the agent user can access. Zero data retention means the external model providers Salesforce uses have agreed not to store the prompts or responses, and not to use them for training, once the response is returned. That trade-off is why I tune masking with the security team rather than masking everything.

q: What is RAG and how does Agentforce use it?

a: RAG stands for retrieval augmented generation. Instead of relying only on what the model learned in training, the system first retrieves relevant pieces of our own content, like knowledge articles, PDFs or policies, and adds them to the prompt, so the model answers from that content. Say a customer asks how long they have to return a sale item. On its own the model might just guess. With RAG, the retriever finds the chunk of our returns policy that covers sale items, that goes into the prompt, and the answer matches our actual policy. In Agentforce, content is chunked and indexed in a Data 360 search index, a retriever finds the most relevant chunks for the user's question, and the agent's knowledge action or a prompt template includes them. This reduces hallucination, keeps answers current without retraining, and lets you cite sources. The Agentforce Data Library makes this much simpler to set up by creating the index and retriever for you.
